17 · The SaaS-pocalypse: same threat, different clocks for equity and debt

What it is. The early-2026 sell-off in seat-based software (SaaS) on the fear that AI agents, which can operate a whole computer and do the work themselves, replace both the users and the software they pay for. It hit equity and debt at once, then spread to any company that looked automatable.

How it works. As told in the Feb 2026 episode: - Trigger. The narrative flipped in two weeks from "when do we see ROI on AI capex?" to "AI will eat the legacy software companies". Kristen ties the trigger to Anthropic's agentic product ("Claude Work" in the transcript) and a widely shared story of an engineer whose agent did his job while he was at lunch. - Credit damage. Citing Bloomberg, Jen says ~$17.7bn of loans to SaaS companies fell into distressed territory in two weeks, a record, taking the sector's distressed total to close to $50bn, the most since 2022. - Contagion by thesis. Money rotated into banks, energy and utilities, then the market hunted "next victims": H&R Block's spreads widened ~80bp in a day; Compass (real-estate brokerage) sold off on the idea that agents replace estate agents. - Equity vs debt clocks. Kristen's key point. An equity multiple values cash flows into perpetuity, so a threat in year 8 hurts the price today. A leverage multiple asks how long it takes to repay. If a SaaS borrower is levered ~2–3x cash flow (her guess), the lender needs only 2–3 years of cash flow before refinancing or repayment. AI eroding revenue over a decade can justify a lower equity multiple and still leave the debt money-good. Jen: debt "is about cash flows over a period of time", and the question is whether AI eats them tomorrow. - Switching costs. Banks stayed on Excel 2003 for years after Excel 2007 changed the shortcuts; Kristen was still teaching on it in 2012, because relearning a "language" costs a desk real productivity. Printed yellow pages lasted until 2019. Schilling's caveat: that stickiness "doesn't last forever"; a tool survives only by adding more value than it charges. - The vendor's view. Macabacus (90,000+ users; ~25% PE/VC, ~20% investment banking) sits in the front office on top of Excel, PowerPoint and Word. Schilling's claim: AI-native tools sit earlier in the workflow (gathering data from filings and data rooms), and his tools sit later (checking, formatting, Excel-to-PowerPoint links that don't break), so the two coexist. He notes the reported Goldman–Anthropic work is aimed at back-office accounting and compliance, not where Macabacus plays.

Business significance. For equity holders the question is terminal value: does the business exist in ten years? For lenders it is the next two to three years of cash flow. Treating them the same is the mispricing. Seat-based pricing is the weak point, because agents reduce both the number of humans and the need for an interface. Tools embedded in a regulated or reputationally sensitive workflow (client deliverables, compliance) are the most defensible.

Forces & impact. Momentum and narrative drove the first leg; valuation (software had traded at "insane multiples") made it violent. Private credit's heavy SaaS exposure (BDCs, PIK loans) means the credit side matters: Medallia (Thoma Bravo, 2021 LBO) defaulted after lenders barred further PIK (with $100m at 10% PIK, the $10m of interest is added to principal, so debt becomes $110m) and the keys went to Apollo and Blackstone. Situational Awareness was short Workday, Adobe, Intuit and Salesforce, which rallied in July 2026 and helped sink it (concept 13). By the SpaceX episode, the SaaS losers were "still licking their wounds" while Nvidia thrived: dispersion again (concept 12).

With vs. without. Without the AI threat, SaaS would be valued as sticky, high-margin annuities and lent to at high leverage, which is what PE did in 2019–21. With it, terminal values compress, refinancing gets harder for the most levered names, and lenders who underwrote a perpetuity at a 2021 multiple own the gap. If agents really did replace seats overnight, the debt would be impaired too. The hosts' view is that switches never flip that fast.

Applies when / Breaks when. The equity/debt distinction holds when leverage is moderate and maturities are near. It breaks for PIK-heavy LBOs at 6–7x, where the payback window is long enough for the threat to arrive, and for software whose only value is the interface an agent can bypass.

Channel example. SAAS-pocalypse, misleading jobs data, and Japanese equities breaking records, feat. Macabacus' CEO; Why a SaaS Company Default (Medallia) is actually a WIN for Private Credit; SpaceX Just Rewrote the Rules of the Stock Market (dispersion aftermath).

Counterpoint. Schilling is a SaaS CEO arguing SaaS is fine. The hosts are loyal users of his product and say so. Both hosts' larger frame is that if AI is good enough to kill software it is coming for every white-collar job, so the market should be pricing "everything is gone", not just SaaS. That is a rhetorical point, not a valuation. jpm software sector spotlight 2026 argues the compression reflects uncertainty rather than deteriorating fundamentals, which fits the equity/debt split. The 2–3x leverage figure is Kristen's guess; sponsor-backed software often runs far higher, which is exactly where the debt argument weakens.

How the concepts connect

AI demand narrative ─► capex guidance ↑ (Google $70bn → $205bn; five hyperscalers ~$800bn for 2026)
        │
        ├─► chips: Nvidia/TSMC/ASML/HBM chokepoints capture rent ─► buyers build ASICs; DeepSeek shows
        │   cheap inference ─► Nvidia buys open-weight distribution (Hugging Face) ─► model margins compress
        │
        ├─► power: flat 24/7 load ─► marginal plant moves up the stack ─► PJM capacity price ~10x
        │   ─► bills ↑ ─► politics ─► "bring your own electrons", moratoria ─► turbine/transformer backlogs
        │   ─► interconnection studies ─► (base rate) ~half of announced capacity never built
        │
        ├─► subsidies: state sales/property tax breaks + 100% bonus depreciation (worth ~$1.8bn PV per
        │   $100bn of chips) ─► "be big right now" ─► spend pulled forward ─► overbuild risk ↑
        │
        └─► funding gap (capex > operating cash flow)
              ├─► equity: Google ~$85bn (common, mandatory convert, ATM); stock-for-stock stack deals
              │   (xAI/X) dilute minority holders
              ├─► corporate bonds ─► spreads widen (Nvidia 40→80, Oracle 215; new 30s +40–60bp) ─► WACC ↑
              ├─► project finance / SPVs (Hyperion: A+, +100bp ≈ $6.5bn; 4-year lease break)
              │   ─► debt off balance sheet, risk not ─► priced as sponsor credit anyway
              ├─► vendor backstops (Nvidia $250bn) + GPU-backed neocloud debt ─► circular revenue
              └─► GAAP useful life sets reported EPS (Burry); cash taxes set by bonus depreciation
                         │
                         ▼
        index concentration (Mag 7 ≈ 1/3 of S&P; mega-IPO inclusion) + low single-name correlation
        ─► hedging demand ─► Oracle CDS crowded; index puts fail under dispersion
        ─► leverage ─► Situational Awareness margin call ─► forced sale ─► KOSPI circuit breakers
                         │
                         ▼
        the payoff test: labor (non-backfill, diamond, junior analysts, revised-down payrolls) and
        software seats (SaaS-pocalypse: equity reprices the perpetuity, debt only the payback window)
        ─► determines whether the model layer can earn enough to justify the IPO valuations
           (Anthropic range ~$2.1–2.25tn on 2028 revenue) that the whole stack is underwritten against

The loop that matters: equity-funded capex is self-limiting; credit-funded capex propagates. Each step down the funding ladder (cash → equity → bonds → SPVs → vendor guarantees → chip-collateral debt) adds reach and adds coupling. Subsidies and bonus depreciation push the whole ladder to move faster. The hosts' three forces of July 2026 (chips, China, credit) hit those coupled links at the same time, and index concentration meant passive investors felt it without having chosen the bet. The SaaS-pocalypse is the same loop seen from the demand side: if AI works, the losers are levered software borrowers, and the question for their lenders is timing, not direction.

Retrieval questions

  1. Why does a data center raise residential power prices more than a factory of the same average draw? It doesn't need to draw more on average. Under marginal pricing, flat 24/7 load lifts the clearing plant in every hour, including the 2–9pm peak when the stack is steepest. All generators, and so all consumers, then pay the higher marginal price.
  2. Meta paid ~1% more on $27bn to use an SPV. Under what conditions is that rational? When keeping the debt off balance sheet protects the rating and debt capacity for a much larger future programme. That is when the higher coupon on one slice is cheaper than repricing all future corporate debt.
  3. A company lengthens GPU useful life from 3 to 6 years. What happens to EPS, EBITDA, cash taxes and a properly built DCF? EPS rises. EBITDA is unchanged. Cash taxes are unchanged under 100% bonus depreciation. The DCF is unchanged unless you also lower your replacement-capex assumption, and that assumption is what actually matters.
  4. Nvidia's spread goes from 40 to 80bp. Roughly what 5-year default probability does the market imply, and why might that overstate reality? About 0.8% × 5 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 6.7% at 40% recovery. Spreads include liquidity and risk premia, so risk-neutral default odds exceed real-world ones.
  5. Why would Nvidia guarantee $250bn of a customer's debt? It converts its own credit rating into ~$350–400bn of locked-in chip and networking orders. The catch: its revenue then partly depends on its own balance sheet, and its credit spread widens.
  6. Why is owning Hugging Face strategic for Nvidia but threatening for closed-model labs? Open weights push the long tail onto Nvidia serving software and hardware, diversifying away from hyperscalers who build their own inference chips. Cheap good-enough models also compress the margin of firms whose product is the model.
  7. Situational Awareness was long/short. Why didn't that protect it? Both legs moved against it (infrastructure and memory fell, shorted chips and software rose). It was 4x levered, so drawdowns triggered daily margin calls. Its index-put hedge didn't track single-name moves under low correlation.
  8. In the Anthropic example, which single assumption moves the range most, and what is methodologically missing? The revenue multiple (each 1x ≈ $200bn of EV). What's missing is discounting 2028 revenue back to today for execution risk and dilution.
  9. Why might half of announced data centers never get built even if capital is abundant? Power, not capital, gates them. Interconnection studies can block or add ~40% to plant costs, equipment backlogs run years, and 1995–2005 shows ~43% of a similar queue cancelled.
  10. Why is "net job loss of 5%" a misleading headline, and what does it imply for macro data? Most of it is roles not backfilled, not layoffs. So it surfaces slowly, first in youth unemployment and margins, and is easy to miss in aggregate payrolls.
  11. Why is Oracle CDS a poor hedge for an AI equity drawdown? It pays only on credit events or spread widening. A 30% AI equity fall with Oracle still solvent leaves the CDS near flat while the premium (130bp/yr) bleeds.
  12. Why do AI labs lean on trade secrets rather than patents, and what follows? Algorithms and AI-generated inventions are largely unpatentable, and patents require disclosure. So the moat lives in people, which makes hiring, non-solicits and inevitable-disclosure lawsuits strategic.
  13. Classic project finance often prices below the sponsor's corporate debt. Why did Meta's Hyperion SPV price ~100bp above Meta's bonds despite an A+ rating? Classic project debt has a 20-year binding offtake contract and lenders who can seize a sellable asset. Hyperion's lease can be walked away from every four years (that is what keeps it off Meta's balance sheet), the SPV is ~92% debt, and the only real credit is Meta's. Lenders were paid for that cancellation option, and possibly overpaid, given PIMCO's 10-point gain.
  14. A state waives sales tax on a data center's chips for 20 years. Why is the cost to the state much larger than the first-year figure? Chips are replaced every ~5 years, so the exemption repeats on each refresh: ~$6bn per cycle on $65bn of chips at ~10% tax, about four times over the term.
  15. Bonus depreciation leaves total tax over five years unchanged. So where is the benefit, and why does it make companies rush? The benefit is time value: tax is deferred, an interest-free loan (~$1.8bn PV per $100bn at 5%). Because a future administration may repeal it, spending now locks in the deferral, which pulls capex forward.
  16. An investor holds an S&P 500 index fund and says she has no AI exposure decision to make. What is wrong with that? Roughly a third of the index is seven AI-linked megacaps and nearly half is tech, and mega-IPO index inclusion adds more. She holds a concentrated thematic bet by default; low single-name correlation means the index can look calm while its parts swing.
  17. AI threatens a software company's revenue over the next decade. Why might its equity fall 40% while its loans should barely move? Equity values cash flows in perpetuity, so a year-8 threat hits today's price. A loan at 2–3x leverage needs only 2–3 years of cash flow to be repaid or refinanced. The argument fails for highly levered or PIK-funded LBOs whose payback window is long enough for the threat to arrive.
  18. January payrolls beat consensus by ~60k, yet Jen called the labor picture worse than expected. Why? Revisions cut 2025's average monthly gain from 49k to 15k, layoffs were at post-crisis highs, and the first print is routinely revised. One strong headline against a large downward revision is weak evidence, and AI's non-backfill effect would show up exactly as slow, revised-down hiring.
